# Joint positive-index restriction at minimal-active stochastic maxima

This is a finite-dimensional variation lemma and its precise tetrahedral incidence consequences. It does not settle the remaining multiple-full-row capacity configurations or OC.

## 1. Several row variations can be funded together

Let phi be positively homogeneous of degree one on the nonnegative orthant R^m. Let X maximize sum_i c_i phi(X_i), c_i>0, over column-stochastic matrices. Choose a maximizer with the minimum number k of nonzero rows. The active rows are linearly independent, as proved in `candidate f62fe2e83b180bf3`: a linear dependence permits proportional row scaling along a two-sided feasible line; homogeneity makes the objective affine and hence constant at a maximum, until one row disappears. Let V be their k-dimensional span. In particular 1 belongs to V, since the active rows sum to 1.

Suppose that for each fully positive C^2 row i in a selected collection, its Hessian has a positive-definite subspace E_i of dimension p_i. Then necessarily

    k+sum_i p_i<=m.                                  (1)

Proof. Map the direct sum of the E_i to R^m/V by sending (v_i) to sum_i v_i modulo V. If sum p_i>m-k, its kernel contains a nonzero tuple. Choose scalars a_j on all active rows with

    sum_i v_i+sum_(j active) a_j X_j=0.

Vary the selected full rows as X_i(t)=(1+t a_i)X_i+t v_i, and every other active row as X_j(t)=(1+t a_j)X_j. All zero rows remain zero. This is feasible in both signs for small t: selected rows are fully positive, while other rows retain their original support and are scaled by positive factors. The column sums are preserved exactly.

The total first derivative is zero by maximality in both signs. Positive homogeneity gives Hess(phi)(X_i) X_i=0, so the second variation is exactly

    sum_i c_i v_i^T Hess(phi)(X_i) v_i>0.

The strict inequality holds because some v_i is nonzero and every selected quadratic form is positive definite on E_i. Pure row scalings contribute no second variation and require no differentiability of those other rows. This contradicts maximality and proves (1).

Equivalently, the exact projective identity phi((1+t a_i)X_i+t v_i)=(1+t a_i)phi(X_i+[t/(1+t a_i)]v_i) proves the same statement using directional second expansions. Thus the lemma is not an assumption that all individual directions can separately be funded.

For m=4: at minimal k=4, one positive-curvature full row is impossible; at k=3, two full rows each having one positive direction are impossible, as is a single full row with a positive plane. At k=2, the same dimension count alone leaves two one-dimensional positive subspaces at equality; the separate exact two-row theorem handles that capacity-support case.

## 2. The threshold Schur correction preserves this funding mechanism

Normalize a full row's proper minimizing threshold to one. Write P(c)=Pr(c dot Xi>=0), where c=1-x, and use g=grad P, H=Hess P, eta=H1. Stationarity gives g dot 1=dP. Suppose

    B=d(d-1)P-1^T H1>0.

For a direction v with g dot v=0 and w=v+l1, direct differentiation of t/F_x(t)^(1/d), followed by its threshold Schur complement, gives

    w^T Hess(phi_d)(x)w
      =-P^(-1/d)/(dP)
          [v^T H v+(eta dot v-l dP)^2/B].             (2)

Thus choosing l=(eta dot v)/(dP) sends every negative cap-curvature direction to a positive capacity-curvature direction. On a negative-definite subspace in g-perpendicular, this linear map is injective: its kernel would make v a constant vector with g dot v=0, hence v=0. Because 1 belongs to V, adding this multiple of 1 preserves whether a direction or a sum of directions belongs to V. This is exactly the correction needed for joint funding.

The complete regularity and nondegeneracy proof is also given independently in `candidate a5d3d44181ebed82`. For clarity, the uncompleted-square expression for the capacity Hessian is

    P^(-1/d)/(dP)
      [-H+(d+1)gg^T/(dP)
            -(eta-dg)(eta-dg)^T/B].                 (3)

Substituting g dot v=0, g dot 1=dP, and 1^T H1=d(d-1)P-B gives (2). Thus no fixed-threshold Hessian is silently substituted for the optimized capacity Hessian.

In d=3 all proper minimizing full rows satisfy the C^2 and B>0 conditions used here. An actual minimizing cap has at least two strictly captured vertices by the facet-positivity identity. It therefore cannot have two boundary vertices and still be proper. A cut through at most one vertex has a cubic knot error, so the cap probability is jointly C^2. Root-volume concavity gives B>=0. If B=0, differentiating the facet-divergence identity would force every facet to obey tF_facet'=2F_facet. For a two-captured cap, deleting one captured vertex leaves a one-vertex triangular cap (possibly with an intercept equal to one), whose ratio root is proportional to t-x_min with x_min>0 and cannot satisfy that equality. For a three-captured cap, deleting the excluded vertex leaves a wholly captured facet, which also cannot satisfy it. Thus B>0. The implicit-function theorem and the unique proper minimum then give a C^2 optimized capacity.

The cited Schur source now also proves B>0 for all d>=2 by logconcavity and an exponential-moment argument. The tetrahedral face proof above remains an independent proof of the case used below; no higher-dimensional incidence classification is inferred from it.

## 3. Central captured vertices and the one-hole geometry

At any positive-weight maximizer, normalized column multipliers equal a common section centroid b for every full row. A surviving one-zero row with hole h forces b_j<=1/3 for j!=h. These are the actual maximizing equations from `candidate 6a014eb26413a72b`.

The archived theorem `candidate 8704554a92158bfc` supplies a strictly negative cap second variation when two strictly captured vertices i,j both have b_i,b_j<=1/3. The actual section centroid makes the cap stationary among planes through b. Equation (2) converts this to a positive capacity direction.

Consider exactly two full rows x,y and one surviving one-zero row z, at a minimal k=3 maximum. Put t_x=b dot x, and similarly t_y,t_z. Since their column sum is 1,

    t_x+t_y+t_z=1.

In the hole column h, z_h=0, so x_h+y_h=1. Hence

    (t_x-x_h)+(t_y-y_h)=-t_z<0.                      (4)

At least one full row therefore strictly excludes h. Its cap has at least two strictly captured vertices; all of them have central b-coordinates because they are not h. It has a positive capacity direction.

If BOTH full rows weakly exclude h, both have positive directions. Equation (1) then reads 3+1+1<=4, a contradiction. The same exclusion applies if b_h<=1/3, since then every coordinate is central, regardless of the incidence at h. These conclusions retain through-vertex cuts: weak exclusion leaves h unavailable as a strictly captured vertex, and the other captured vertices are strict.

The remaining one-hole case is explicit: b_h>1/3, one full row strictly captures h, and the other strictly excludes it. The latter has a positive direction; the former has not been shown here to have one. A single positive direction at k=3 does not contradict (1), and it is not assumed to lie in V individually.

For three full rows and no positive zero row (still k=3), two positive-curvature full rows suffice for exclusion, but this note does not assert that two always exist. For k=4, a single positive-curvature row suffices. Centrality of b cannot be presumed in either of these cases.

The exact row-level limitation is recorded in `candidate 61582452a1450270`: a positive proper full row may have no positive Hessian direction when its section centroid is noncentral. Thus the unresolved incidence configurations require actual additional geometry, not merely an index count.

## 4. Four active rows cannot include a full row

We now prove the needed shared-incidence statement, rather than assume universal positive curvature of a single row.

First, in a quadrilateral tetrahedral section any two barycentric centroid coordinates greater than 1/3 belong to the same cut side. Use positive diagonal parameters X,Y on one side and Z,W on the other, with T=X+Y+Z+W. The actual centroid formulas give

    3b_X>1 iff YX^2>ZW(T+X),
    3b_Z>1 iff WZ^2>XY(T+Z).

If both held, multiplication and cancellation of the positive factor XYZW would give XZ>(T+X)(T+Z), impossible. Relabeling gives the assertion for any opposite-side pair. This even excludes both opposite-side coordinates being at least 1/3.

A proper minimizing full-row cap has at least two strictly captured vertices. If it has three, its section is the triangle cutting off the sole excluded vertex, and each captured coordinate of the section centroid is an edge intercept strictly less than one divided by three. Thus only the excluded coordinate can exceed 1/3. If the section passes through a vertex, its margin pattern is (+,+,-,0); the boundary coordinate is exactly 1/3, each strictly captured coordinate is strictly less than 1/3, and again only the excluded coordinate can exceed 1/3. These statements follow by taking the centroid of the three actual section vertices. There is no untracked boundary incidence.

Now let a minimal-active positive-weight maximizer in the tetrahedral problem have k=4 and at least one full row. Nontrivial full-cut rows have already been excluded by `candidate 78b95c208ba2d374`. A saturated full-cut row has a unit capacity vector and is already paid; moreover its other nonzero rows would all be supported in one column, contradicting four-row independence. Hence all full rows here have proper minima and common section centroid b.

Every other nonzero row has exactly one zero, by the fractional-power perturbation exclusion in the section-centroid source. Rows sharing a hole can be merged without changing the objective, contrary to the chosen minimal number of active rows. In particular the surviving holes are distinct.

Let I={j:b_j>1/3}. Its size is at most two.

If I is empty, every full row has a strictly captured central pair and thus positive curvature. Equation (1) already contradicts k=4.

If I={h}, every one-zero row, if present, must have its hole at h: otherwise its missing-entry restriction would force b_h<=1/3. By minimality there is at most one such row. For each active row x_i put t_i=b dot x_i. Column stochasticity gives

    sum_i (t_i-x_ih)=0.

Any one-zero row contributes the strictly positive margin t_i at h. Consequently not all full rows can strictly capture h. Some full row weakly excludes it; that row's at least two strictly captured vertices are central. It has positive curvature, again contradicting (1).

If |I|=2, no one-zero row can exist, because its missing-entry restriction allows at most one noncentral coordinate. Thus all four rows are full. By the preceding incidence facts, every section is a strict quadrilateral and places the two noncentral coordinates on the same side. Fix either noncentral coordinate h. No row can put h on its boundary, since a boundary section coordinate equals 1/3. The balanced-margin equation sum_i(t_i-x_ih)=0 therefore forces at least one negative margin. That row excludes BOTH noncentral vertices, so it captures the two central vertices. Its positive curvature contradicts (1).

All cases lead to a contradiction. Hence a minimal-active tetrahedral maximizer with four nonzero rows has no full row. The existing zero-row boundary support theorem then applies to that configuration. This is an actual shared-row result; it does not contradict the isolated concave-capacity row calibration.

After this reduction, the multiple-full-row configurations not paid in this note have k=3: three full rows, or two full rows and one one-zero row. The latter has already been reduced in Section 3 to a unique noncentral hole that is captured by exactly one of the two full rows. The exact two-row theorem handles k<=2, and the separate one-full-row results handle every merged k=3 one-full configuration. No conclusion about the two remaining k=3 configurations is inferred here.
